title: HTTP: The Language of the Web
summary: You'll be able to read raw HTTP requests and responses, choose the right methods, status codes and caching headers, and explain what HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 improved.

questions.prompt: What's the difference between `401 Unauthorized` and `403 Forbidden`? And in general, what does a 4xx code tell a client compared with a 5xx code?
questions.hint: Whose fault is it, and would trying again help?
keyPoints: 401: the request lacks valid authentication (not logged in / bad or expired token)
403: the user is authenticated but not allowed to do this
4xx means the client's request is wrong; retrying the same request unchanged won't help (except 429 after waiting)
5xx means the server failed; the request may succeed if retried later (with backoff)
Monitoring treats 5xx as the service's fault and alerts on it

questions.prompt: Explain **safe** and **idempotent** HTTP methods. Classify GET, POST, PUT and DELETE. Why does this matter when a client's request times out?
questions.hint: What happens if the same request is executed twice?
keyPoints: Safe: doesn't change server state (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS)
Idempotent: repeating it has the same effect as doing it once (GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent)
POST is neither safe nor idempotent: retrying can create duplicates (e.g. two orders)
After a timeout the client doesn't know if the request happened; idempotent requests can be retried safely
For POST, use an idempotency key header so the server can detect and dedupe retries

questions.prompt:
You're setting caching headers for three responses:

1. `/static/app.8f3a2c.js` (filename contains a content hash)
2. `/index.html` (changes whenever you deploy)
3. `/api/me/bank-balance`

What `Cache-Control` (and other) headers would you use for each, and why?
questions.hint: Which of these can never change at the same URL? Which must always be fresh? Which must never be stored?
keyPoints: Hashed JS: `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` — the URL changes when content changes, so cache forever (browser and CDN)
index.html: `no-cache` (or a short max-age) plus ETag/Last-Modified so clients revalidate and get 304 when unchanged; it references the new hashed files after a deploy
Bank balance: `no-store` (and private) — sensitive, user-specific data must not be stored in shared or browser caches
Explains that no-cache means 'revalidate before use', not 'don't cache'
Mentions public vs private: shared caches/CDNs must not cache user-specific responses

questions.prompt:
A page needs **60** small assets from one host. RTT is **80 ms** and each asset transfers in negligible time once requested. The connections are already open.

1. With HTTP/1.1 (6 connections per host, one request at a time per connection), roughly how long does fetching all assets take?
2. With HTTP/2 over one connection?
3. What would make HTTP/2 lose its advantage on a bad mobile network?
questions.hint: Each request on an HTTP/1.1 connection costs one round trip and can't overlap with another on the same connection.
keyPoints: HTTP/1.1: 60 / 6 = 10 sequential rounds × 80 ms ≈ 800 ms
HTTP/2: all 60 requests multiplexed at once ≈ 1 RTT ≈ 80 ms (plus transfer time)
The gain comes from multiplexing many streams over one connection
On lossy networks, TCP head-of-line blocking stalls all HTTP/2 streams when one packet is lost; HTTP/3 over QUIC avoids this
questions.answer:
1. `60 / 6 = 10` rounds × 80 ms ≈ **800 ms**.
2. All 60 go out together: about **1 RTT ≈ 80 ms** plus transfer time.
3. Packet loss: HTTP/2 rides on one TCP connection, so a single lost packet stalls every stream (TCP head-of-line blocking). HTTP/3/QUIC fixes this with per-stream reliability.

questions.hint: Check the method, the URL, and every status code.
keyPoints: Deleting via GET is wrong: GET must be safe (crawlers/prefetchers/caches may trigger it); use `DELETE /users/:id`
Not found should be 404, not 200 with an error body
Successful delete: 204 No Content (or 200 with a body)
Successful create: 201 Created, ideally with a `Location: /users/<id>` header
Errors: 400/422 for invalid input, 409 for conflicts (e.g. duplicate email), 500 for unexpected failures; don't leak raw internal error messages

questions.prompt: HTTP is stateless, yet users stay logged in across hundreds of requests. Describe how a cookie-based session works end to end, which cookie attributes you'd set and why, and what changes when you have 20 app servers behind a load balancer.
questions.hint: Who stores the state, and where does each server look it up?
keyPoints: On login the server creates a session (random unguessable ID → user data) and sends `Set-Cookie: session=<id>`
The browser automatically sends `Cookie: session=<id>` on later requests; the server looks the ID up to identify the user
Attributes: HttpOnly (no JS access, limits XSS theft), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite=Lax/Strict (CSRF protection), a reasonable Max-Age/expiry
With many servers, store sessions in a shared store (e.g. Redis) so any server can handle any request, keeping app servers stateless; sticky sessions are an inferior alternative
Alternative: signed tokens (e.g. JWT) carry state themselves, trading easy revocation for no lookup
